title: The Ra'avad of Posquières
content:
The Ra'avad of Posquières
This article surveys the life, literary output, and historical influence of Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières (the Third Ra'avad), who was a key figure in 12th-century French Jewry. The text emphasizes his formidable interpretive and halakhic enterprise, which includes his famous work "Ba'alei ha-Nefesh" alongside his critical objections to Maimonides, which were intended to preserve the dynamism of the Talmud against the attempt to fix a decided and monolithic halakha. Beyond the halakhic aspect, the source analyzes his theological disputes on the subjects of providence, reward and punishment, and the corporeality of God, presenting his complex position that combines rational scholarship with mystical inspiration. Finally, the article establishes the Ra'avad's standing as a central link in the chain of transmission of Kabbalistic teaching, since his close circle and his students were the ones who shaped and disseminated the foundations of the esoteric teaching from the region of Provence to the other centers of Torah.
The Work, Torah Teaching, and Halakhic Legacy of the Ra'avad of Posquières
The region of Provence in the twelfth century served as a unique space of mediation between the scholarly world of the Tosafists of northern France and the centralized and philosophical Torah centers of Spain and North Africa. In this dynamic spiritual environment worked Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières (the Third Ra'avad, also known as the "author of the objections" or "the Ra'avad of Kiryat Yearim"), who is regarded as one of the great Rishonim who shaped the face of learning and halakhic ruling for the generations to come.[1, 2, 3] The Ra'avad's work encompassed all areas of Torah creativity: interpretation of the Talmud, composition of halakhic monographs, polemics against decisive codes, and a crucial role in formulating the beginnings of the teaching of Kabbalah in Europe.[3, 4, 5]
Biography, Institutions, and Interactions with the Sages of His Generation
The Ra'avad was born in Narbonne in Provence around the year 4880 (approximately 1120) and died on 26 Kislev 4959 (1198), having lived about 74 years.[1, 2, 3] He acquired his early Torah education in the yeshiva of Narbonne under Rabbi Moshe ben Rabbi Yosef Maron HaLevi.[3] He then studied under Rabbi Avraham Av Beit Din (the Second Ra'avad, author of Sefer ha-Eshkol), who became his principal teacher and even gave him his daughter in marriage.[2, 3] He completed his course of study in the yeshiva of Lunel under Rabbi Meshullam ben Rabbi Yaakov of Lunel.[3] After a period during which he lived in the city of Nîmes, he moved to Posquières (today called Vauvert, France), which was called by the Jews "Kiryat Yearim," and there he served as rabbi and head of a yeshiva for most of his days.[2, 3]
The Ra'avad was a man of great personal wealth, and this wealth enabled him to support the students of his yeshiva in Posquières from his private funds, which made the place a magnet for many sages and established his standing as the foremost of the sages of Provence, called by them "the lion of the group."[3] The circumstances of his life were at times affected by political events and local wars; the Meiri relates that because of a war that broke out in Posquières, the Ra'avad was compelled to leave the city, and on his way back to Narbonne he passed through Carcassonne, acceded to the request of the townspeople to settle there temporarily, and there he composed his work "Hilkhot Lulav."[3]
The Ra'avad's relations with the sages of his generation were characterized by stormy dialectic. Particularly complex relations existed between him and Rabbi Zerachia HaLevi (the Razah, Baal HaMaor), with whom he conducted sharp halakhic debates, such as the exchange of letters "Divrei ha-Rivot," dealing with the laws of oaths in tractate Bava Metzia [3, 6], as well as the Razah's objections to the book "Ba'alei ha-Nefesh," which were called "Sela ha-Machlokot."[7] Nevertheless, the Ra'avad displayed a deep commitment to the halakhic tradition of the Rif, whom he admiringly called "the Rav," and composed the book "Katuv Sham" to defend the Rif from the sharp criticism of the Baal HaMaor.[3]
The Ra'avad raised a series of students who constituted the central link in the transmission of the teaching of Provence and the beginnings of Kabbalah to the sages of Spain and Catalonia.[2, 5]
The Ra'avad's Literary Corpus: Halakha, Interpretation, and Polemic
The scope of the Ra'avad's writing attests to methodological versatility, from local commentaries to systematic monographs reflecting a comprehensive religious philosophy of life.
Halakha, the Forbidden and the Permitted, and Family Life
His most prominent halakhic book is "Ba'alei ha-Nefesh," a halakhic-moral work in seven gates (sha'arim) dealing with the laws of niddah and marital life.[7, 9] The first six gates are devoted to meticulous scholarly discussion of the laws of distancing (hirhuk), menstrual cycles (vesetot), laws of local separation (such as the law of a guest who separates from his wife when they have no private room), the prohibition of marital relations by day or by the light of a candle, and the covering of sacred books.[7, 9] The seventh gate, "Sha'ar ha-Kedushah" (The Gate of Holiness), deals with directing thought and consciousness at the time of the act, out of a conception that a person's sanctification in his thoughts brings about the birth of children of spiritual stature.[7, 10] The book gained a canonical status, and served as a basis for the works of the Ramban, the Rashba, the Rosh, and Rabbi Yosef Karo.[7]
Alongside this book, the Ra'avad composed "Issur Mashehu," a work dealing with the laws of nullification of prohibitions in mixtures, which was written while his teacher Meshullam HaKohen of Lunel was still alive and was based on a similar book composed by his teacher.[3]
Interpretation of the Talmud and the Halakhic Midrashim
The Ra'avad wrote a comprehensive commentary on many tractates of the Babylonian Talmud, but most of them were lost, among them the commentaries on tractates Berakhot, Shabbat, Eruvin, Ta'anit, Mo'ed Katan, Ketubot, Kiddushin, Bava Metzia, and Bava Batra.[2] Of his Talmudic commentaries, those that survived are mainly the ones on tractates Bava Kamma, Avodah Zarah, and Kinnim.[2, 3] The printed commentary on tractate Tamid that is attributed to him in the accepted literature is not his.[2]
In the field of the halakhic midrashim, the Ra'avad was a pioneer in writing a systematic and comprehensive commentary on the book "Sifra" (Torat Kohanim) on the book of Leviticus.[4, 11] This commentary is characterized by sharp philological and scholarly analysis, which resolves internal contradictions and clarifies the homilies of the Sages, and it was one of the first attempts to decipher this midrashic collection independently.[11]
Polemic and Kabbalah
In addition to the book "Katuv Sham" in defense of the Rif [3], the Ra'avad composed objections to his teacher Rabbi Yosef ibn Plat that did not appear in print.[3] Likewise, the collection "Temim De'im" gathers halakhic responsa and rulings of the Ra'avad alongside fragments of objections.[3] In the homiletic literature there survive a "Sermon for Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur" (Bodleian Library manuscript) and remnants of a sermon for Passover.[3] The well-known Kabbalistic commentary on "Sefer Yetzirah" that was attributed to him throughout the generations is not his work, but was composed by the Spanish Kabbalist Rabbi Yosef ben Shalom Ashkenazi.[3, 12]
The Ra'avad's Objections to Maimonides: A Methodological Dispute and the Philosophy of Halakhic Ruling
The Ra'avad's most influential literary enterprise, which gave him an eternal standing in the history of Jewish learning, is his objections to Maimonides' great work, the "Mishneh Torah."[13] Behind these local comments lay a fundamental dispute over the nature of halakhic ruling, the place of the judge, and the future of the study of the Oral Torah.
The Essence of the Opposition to the Monolithic Code
Maimonides sought to bring about a revolution in halakhic writing by creating a code that presents a decided and exclusive halakha, without sources and without mention of the dissenting opinions or the disputes of the Geonim who preceded him.[13] The Ra'avad identified in this method a grave danger to the chain of transmission.[13] In his view, one must not rule halakha without knowing its Talmudic source, since the absence of the source prevents the student from criticizing the ruling, from comparing cases, and may lead to grave errors in the application of the law.[13]
The Ra'avad held that the author's duty is to present to the student and the judge the variety of opinions, in order to enable them to decide among them.[13] He emphasized that a judge who was aware that a great sage had interpreted the matters differently might have retracted from his ruling, and wondered why he should abandon his tradition and his sources in favor of Maimonides' subjective choice of a single opinion in a place where the Geonim were divided.[13] In addition, behind the objections stood a deep cultural concern that learners would abandon altogether dialectical analysis of the Talmud and focus solely on memorizing final codes.[13]
The Style of Writing and the Meaning of Its Sharpness
The style of the objections combines uncompromising scholarly firmness with great respect for Maimonides.[13] The Ra'avad opens every objection with the initials aleph-aleph ("Amar Avraham"—"Abraham said").[13] Alongside the use of particularly sharp expressions, there are places where he affirms Maimonides' words and even praises him in warm terms, such as his appreciation in the laws of kilayim: "He performed a great task in gathering and collecting in his hands all of these."[13]
Sages of later generations offered various explanations for the Ra'avad's linguistic sharpness:
Rabbi Gedalya ibn Yachya (author of "Shalshelet ha-Kabbalah") suggested that the expressions were meant to express contempt for Maimonides, a conjecture that was rejected by most scholars and commentators.[13]
The Rem'a of Fano conjectured that the sharpness was intended to distance learners from Maimonides' philosophical book, the "Guide of the Perplexed," but this conjecture was rejected chronologically, since it seems that the Ra'avad had already died before the Guide of the Perplexed was disseminated in Provence.[13]
The Maharam Chagiz argued that the Ra'avad's purpose was to "cool down" the excessive public enthusiasm for the Mishneh Torah, in order to prevent it from becoming an exclusive and fixed law and to leave an opening of interpretive freedom for the generations to come.[13]
In the name of Rabbi Chaim of Brisk it is reported that the degree of sharpness in the language of an objection directly and mathematically reflects the degree of the Ra'avad's substantive opposition to the content of the proposed ruling.[13]
The Influence of the Objections on Halakhic Reception and Ruling
The objections became an integral part of the study of the Mishneh Torah, and in almost all editions of Maimonides they are printed alongside the text.[4] They encouraged the creation of an extensive defensive literature on the part of the "armor-bearers" (nos'ei ha-kelim) of Maimonides, such as the "Kesef Mishneh" of Rabbi Yosef Karo, who came to the defense of Maimonides and argued that the student may rely on his rulings even without investigating the sources.[13] The question of the Ra'avad's silence in his objections aroused a methodological discussion: whereas Rabbi Chaim Benveniste (in his book "Keneset ha-Gedolah") saw silence as blanket agreement, other sages proved that there are cases in which the Ra'avad's opinion in his other works is contrary to Maimonides and yet he did not object to him.[3, 13] Rabbi Yosef Qafih held that one should not see silence as agreement and that one should not learn practical halakha directly from the objections, but rather the Ra'avad's role was to serve as a "revealer to the student" of the existence of an alternative interpretive tradition.[13]
An In-Depth Study of the Theological and Conceptual Objections in the Laws of Repentance
One of the most important sections in the Ra'avad's objections is found in the Book of Knowledge, and especially in the chapters of the Laws of Repentance.[14, 15] In these chapters the Ra'avad confronts Maimonides' rationalist and philosophical method, and defends the faith-based, realist, and rabbinic traditions against philosophical abstraction that in his view threatens the foundations of simple faith.
The Corporeality of God and the Boundaries of Heresy (Laws of Repentance 3:7)
Maimonides ruled that there are five who are called heretics (minim), among them one who says that there is one Master but He is a body and has a form.[16] This ruling means that one who mistakenly believes in corporeality loses his share in the World to Come and is defined as a denier.[16] The Ra'avad objected to this sharply, combining religious tolerance and sociological realism:
"Abraham said: And why did he call him a heretic (min)? Many who are greater and better than he followed this thought, according to what they saw in the Scriptures, and even more so in what they saw in the words of aggadot that confuse the mind."[16, 17]
The Ra'avad clarifies that although the true essence of the faith is that God has no body and no likeness of a body, a person who believes that God is a body out of a simple understanding of the language of the verses and the midrashim as written should not be defined as a "heretic" (min).[16, 17] An interpretive error stemming from limited comprehension should not remove a person from the community of Israel.[16]
This position generated a broad theological controversy:
Sefer ha-Ikkarim: Rabbi Yosef Albo used the Ra'avad's words as central evidence that one who errs in his study of the principles of the Torah out of sincere inquiry and does not intend to rebel against the tradition is not defined as a heretic or denier.[16] The author of the book "Be'er Sheva" extended this principle to determine that one who holds the belief in the resurrection of the dead by virtue of tradition but mistakenly thinks that it is not alluded to in the Torah has a share in the World to Come.[15, 16]
Abravanel and Kovetz Ma'amarim (Collected Essays): By contrast, Don Isaac Abravanel (in his book "Rosh Amanah") entirely rejected the Ra'avad's position by means of the "parable of the deadly poison"—just as poison destroys the physical body even if eaten inadvertently and by mistake, so heresy and corporealism corrupt the soul ontologically and prevent life in the World to Come regardless of the believer's intention.[16] Abravanel distinguished between heresy out of ignorance (for which there is an opening of repentance if his opinion is set straight) and heresy out of rebelliousness (like Elisha ben Abuyah).[16] Rabbi Elchanan Wasserman held a similar position and determined that "one who denies inadvertently is a denier," since the corruption of opinions impedes the soul in an inherent manner.[16]
Knowledge and Choice (Laws of Repentance 5:6)
In dealing with the question of the relationship between God's foreknowledge and man's free choice, Maimonides argues that we have no power to grasp the essence of the Creator's knowledge, and returns the matter to faith.[15] The Ra'avad sharply attacks Maimonides' decision to present the difficulty without a satisfactory solution:
"This author did not follow the practice of the sages, that a person does not begin something that he does not know how to complete; and he began with difficult questions and left the matter as a difficulty and referred it back to faith; and it would have been better for him to leave the matter to the simplicity of the simple, and not to arouse their hearts and leave their minds in doubt."[15]
The Ra'avad warns against the educational damage of arousing doubts in the hearts of simple believers.[15] He proposes an alternative solution that combines a cosmological-astrological conception: the Creator delegated the governance of the natural world to the system of the constellations (mazalot), and His knowledge of the future is similar to the knowledge of the astrologers who observe the stars.[15] However, since the Creator gave man intellect and free choice, man has the power to overcome the system of the constellations and to be freed from the decree.[15] Thus, God's knowledge does not determine man's actual deeds.[15]
The Nature of the World to Come and the Resurrection of the Dead (Laws of Repentance 8:2)
Maimonides held that in the World to Come there is no body or physical form, but only souls.[15] The Ra'avad objected to this forcefully and argued that this position is close to a denial of the resurrection of the dead in bodies.[15] To establish his position that the righteous will stand in their bodies, the Ra'avad presents four central Talmudic sources:
Tractate Ketubot (111b): The statement that the righteous are destined to rise in their garments, learned a fortiori from the grain of wheat.[15]
Tractate Shabbat (114a): The instructions of sages to their sons not to bury them in white or black garments, lest they merit to rise at the resurrection of the dead and be ashamed of their clothing.[15]
Tractate Sanhedrin (92a): The statement that the righteous whom the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to revive do not return to their dust but rise in their bodies.[15]
Tractate Sanhedrin (91b): The statement that the righteous rise at the resurrection of the dead with their blemishes (so that they will be recognized) and then are healed.[15]
The Ra'avad concludes from this that the World to Come includes a refined physical reality, in which the Creator will place the bodies of the righteous in a strong and healthy state like the bodies of the angels and like the body of Elijah the Prophet, and the crowns and feasts will be literal and not merely a parable.[15]
Additional Comments on the Laws of Repentance
The feast in the World to Come (Laws of Repentance 8:4): Maimonides interpreted the "feast of the righteous" as only a parable.[15] The Ra'avad mocks this: "And if this is the feast, there is no cup of blessing here. And silence would have been better for him."[15]
The destruction of the world (Laws of Repentance 8:8): The Ra'avad objects to Maimonides, who appears to deny the tradition that the world is destined to be destroyed and renewed, basing himself on the saying "The world will exist for six thousand years, and one will be desolate" (Sanhedrin 97a).[15]
Publicizing sin (Laws of Repentance 2:5): Maimonides dealt with the limits of publicizing repentance. The Ra'avad qualifies and distinguishes: in the case of publicly known and exposed transgressions, even though they are not between man and his fellow, the sinner is obligated to publicize his repentance publicly in order to be ashamed before the public, just as the sin was open.[15]
The interpretation of "shor aniyim" (Laws of Repentance 4:3): Maimonides counted among those who hinder repentance "one who eats the ox of the poor (shor aniyim)." The Ra'avad proposes a philological and textual correction, explaining that the correct reading is "shod aniyim" (the plunder of the poor) with a dalet and not "shor" with a resh, and the meaning is one who presses the poor person with his debt until he is compelled to sell him his lands or movable property for less than their true value.[15]
Kabbalah, Divine Inspiration, and the Uniqueness of the Provence Circle
Alongside his meticulous halakhic and interpretive engagement, the Ra'avad worked in the turning-point period in which the historical teaching of Kabbalah began to appear in Provence, in parallel with the appearance of "Sefer ha-Bahir" around the year 1180.[18] The Ra'avad made a decisive contribution to the establishment of a mystical consciousness within the halakhic study hall, while integrating heavenly revelations into his practical halakhic ruling.
In his books there appear statements presenting an unconventional epistemological conception in the world of halakha, according to which the Holy Spirit constitutes a legitimate source of knowledge for deciding doubts:
"All that has been revealed to me of the secret of the Lord to those who fear Him."[3]
"So they showed me from Heaven."[3]
"The Holy Spirit has already appeared in our study hall for several years."[3]
According to the testimony of Rabbi Chaim Vital, the meaning of the expression "the secret of the Lord to those who fear Him" in the context of the Ra'avad is that he had a revelation of Elijah, a characterization that illustrates his extraordinary spiritual level, although the Maharam ibn Chaviv disagrees with this specific identification and prefers to see in it a level of divine inspiration arising from labor in the Torah.[3]
The Ra'avad developed a mystical doctrine according to which the voice of the righteous person who engages in Torah or prayer has a real (substantive) existence outside the person.[19] These voices become holy entities that mediate revelations of the souls of the righteous or divine powers.[19] This conception finds practical expression in the "Sha'ar ha-Kedushah" in the book "Ba'alei ha-Nefesh," in which moral conduct and holiness at the time of intimacy serve as a vehicle for drawing down the Holy Spirit and for the attachment of thought to the root of the soul.[10, 19]
The Ra'avad's esoteric teaching was systematized and disseminated through the circle of his family and students in Provence.[5] His son, Rabbi Isaac the Blind (Sagi Nahor), was regarded by many Kabbalists, such as Rabbeinu Bachya, as the "father of Kabbalah" and as the one who shaped the skeleton of the early doctrine of the sefirot.[5, 8] The students of Rabbi Isaac, Rabbi Ezra and Rabbi Azriel, were the ones who transmitted the Kabbalah of Provence to the sages of Gerona, foremost among them the Ramban.[8] Through this chain of transmission, Kabbalah turned from a closed intuitive experience into a speculative and practical teaching accepted by the great transmitters of the halakhic tradition of Spanish Jewry.[5, 8]
Comparative Analysis of the Theological and Methodological Disputes

Summary and Conclusions
The Torah work of Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières presents a model of multidimensional spiritual leadership that combined scholarly conservatism with methodological and mystical revolutionism. The Ra'avad did not act as an isolated spring but as a wealthy and influential community leader, who could afford complete intellectual independence vis-à-vis the great figures of his generation and vis-à-vis the decisive model that Maimonides sought to instill.[3, 13]
His objections to Maimonides prevented the transformation of halakha into a static code, and preserved the vitality of the Oral Torah as a dynamic system based on the study of the original topics, pluralism of opinions, and interpretive freedom for the local judge.[13] His moderate theological position on the corporeality of God attests to a broad human outlook that distinguishes between rebellious heresy and error stemming from human limitation of comprehension or simple literal interpretation, and opened a window to religious tolerance and a profound philosophical discussion of the boundaries of faith for the generations to come.[16]
At the same time, the foundations of Kabbalah that the Ra'avad laid in Provence, which were systematized through his son Rabbi Isaac the Blind (Sagi Nahor) and his students, showed how Jewish mysticism grew not as an anarchic movement seeking to break through the boundaries of the law, but out of the most rigorous halakhic study hall.[5, 8] The combination that the Ra'avad created between halakhic precision, pioneering midrashic interpretation, independence vis-à-vis codification, and openness to divine inspiration and to "the secret of the Lord to those who fear Him," established his figure as an eternal link in shaping the figure of the Torah scholar and in the development of rabbinic and mystical Judaism in the Middle Ages and the modern era.[1, 3]
